segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the city of Schwäbisch Hall, my gracious and beloved lords and superiors.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent and wise lords: I first offer Your Worships my entirely willing and diligent service, my gracious and beloved lords and superiors. Your Worships know that almighty, eternal God truly created the heavens, the sun and moon, together with the other stars, for the particular benefit of human beings and this lower world. In these created things one finds what is to happen among the creatures of this mortal world. Accordingly Aristotle, the [principal—reading uncertain] master of natural philosophy, says: This lower world is joined to the higher bodies of heaven so that all its power may be governed by them. Ptolemy, [highly esteemed—reading uncertain] in astrology, also repeatedly attests this, saying: This lower world is subject to the stars of heaven, from which one may obtain knowledge of great future events, of the things that are to happen by nature, and thus learn them with certainty. For through the ordering of the heavenly bodies and their revolutions, divine power, wisdom and goodness are revealed in governing these lower, earthly bodies through the higher ones. The royal prophet David in his book of Psalms, and likewise the philosopher Plato, say and maintain that, by God's will, these things are written in the heavens as in a book for us to know. John of Damascus and Albert the Great, together with other Christian teachers, also firmly maintain this, saying: Almighty God has made the heavens like a skin or a book in which all events [reading uncertain] and future things that are to happen by nature in this lower world are written. Human beings are permitted to read it: whoever can read it may do so.

Such influence and inclination of the stars can indeed be known through the natural art of astrology. Therefore it is [right—reading uncertain] and true to believe that almighty God extended the lives of the holy fathers, namely Noah, Abraham and others, over many years so that they might thoroughly understand the lofty and useful art of astrology for the good of humankind. Ptolemy, Albumasar, Hermes and many others highly learned in this art have also been gifted with profound natural understanding, enabling them, through long effort and labor, to investigate the true courses of the stars and planets and their nature, together with the twelve stars and houses in the heavens. In them all the events and future occurrences of this lower world are impressed and contained, for prosperity or [destruction—reading uncertain], through those same houses from one to another.

Through the planets also, as they pass among the fixed stars, and through their bad and good aspects, all are led, governed and guided: [now—reading uncertain] toward good, joy or prosperity, and then toward evil, such as war, rebellion, pestilence, illnesses, dearth and the like. Consequently a person finds himself healthy, prosperous and joyful for a time, and at another time ill, sorrowful and beset by great adversity.

On these grounds, by the grace of almighty God, I have composed and written, with no small diligence, a prognostication, commonly called a Practica, in honor of Your Worships and for the benefit of all humankind. Its purpose is to enable people to pay attention to future events, to guard against dangers and the like as far as possible, and to endure future misfortune, some of which they may perhaps avoid [construction uncertain]. That this is possible is openly attested by Ptolemy, most renowned in astrology, in the Book of a Hundred Sayings: A person can and may, by and with the aid of astrology, prevent much evil here on earth and avert much harm to human beings arising from the influence of the stars.

I have wished to make known that inclination and influence for this coming year 1528, drawing on the counsel of those most experienced in this art, and to have it disseminated in print below—not because things must always happen in this way, but as a warning. I therefore humbly ask Your Worships graciously to accept from me this judgment, briefly set out and composed for Your Worships' particular pleasure. To you I herewith commend myself in humble, dutiful and obedient submission. Given on the [twelfth?] day of July, in the year [1527?].

Your Worships' obedient servant,
Dr. Antonius Brelochs.

notes.text: The civic title Stetmaister is conventionally rendered mayors; its precise local office should be distinguished from a modern mayoralty. E.E.W. is rendered Your Worships as an approximate collective English civic honorific addressed to the magistrates and council.

Astronomei/Astronomia is generally rendered astrology in this predictive context. Early modern usage overlapped the modern disciplines of astronomy and astrology; the translation does not imply that Brelochs used the modern distinction. Zunaygung/neigung is rendered inclination, and einfluß influence.

The German working transcription marks Hauptlich (A2r, line 10), geehrest (line 12), gültlichen (line 27), zurstöligkait (line 36), and Yetzo (line 38) as unclear. Their tentative English renderings are bracketed. Natural philosophy is the contextual sense of natürlich in Aristotle's title; destruction is the probable contextual sense of the unclear word opposed to prosperity.

At A2r, line 23, the working transcription reads alle geschrybt, a syntactically difficult reading. The scan appears compatible with geschicht (events), but a fresh collation is needed. The translation therefore marks events as uncertain rather than silently treating a correction as established. Likewise the twelve stars in line 34 may refer to zodiacal signs, but the translation retains the working transcription's steren rather than substituting signs without notice.

Damascenus is rendered John of Damascus, and Albertus der groß Albert the Great. Ptolemy, Albumasar and Hermes follow conventional English forms of the names cited. The translation reports Brelochs's attributions; it does not verify their source passages or authorship. His Book of a Hundred Sayings is the work traditionally attributed to Ptolemy, commonly called the Centiloquium.

The uncertain xij and xxvij in the subscription are tentatively rendered twelfth and 1527. Hewmonadt is July. The forecast year 1528 and the dedication's apparent date in 1527 are distinguished. The source's abbreviated Anno &c. supplies only xxvij; the full century is expanded contextually and remains bracketed with the uncertain year.

At A2v, lines 2–3, das ander etwan können vermeyden is ambiguous in the provisional transcription. The English tentatively takes it to mean that some misfortune may be avoided; alternatives include misfortune that others may avoid or other misfortunes that may be avoided. The broad contrast of enduring and averting harm is clear, but this clause requires collation.

segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the city of Schwäbisch Hall, my gracious and beloved lords in authority.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent, and wise sirs: my most willing and diligent service to Your Worships first of all, my gracious and beloved lords in authority. Until now, German astrological practicas have had a very bad reputation among people of every station, high and low, and have in many ways been regarded as little books of lies. Now it is certainly true that, if the art of astrology and its practitioners wished to extend their reach so far as to encroach upon the power, wisdom, and providence of the almighty Lord and God, and to confine and compel God's omnipotence within their rules, ordinances, and statutes, then no honorable, devout Christian could be surprised that such a bad reputation had arisen concerning the practica. But anyone more disposed to reflect upon the truth than to disparage severely an art of which he has neither experience nor knowledge would surely recognize that no honorable mind and heart would rise up so presumptuously against our almighty Creator and seek, through astrology or any other art and wisdom, to overpower God's eternal providence. For, according to the teaching of the holy apostle Paul, we know well that God's almighty power cannot be circumscribed, that his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable, that no one has been his counselor, but that all things are from him, through him, and to him. We also know that everything we intend to undertake and do, in word and deed, should begin and end neither in the name of the course of the heavens nor on the basis of the wisdom of the art of astrology, but in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom alone God his heavenly Father has appointed and ordained to be our wisdom—indeed, a treasury of all divine knowledge.

Nevertheless, our almighty Lord and God first created the heavens by his word and power, and in the heavens the sun and moon, as well as [other?] stars; and until the end of the world he will powerfully move them and, as I might call it, cause them to revolve. Moreover, he has so finely and orderly arranged the sun and the growth of the earth in relation to one another that anyone endowed with even ordinary human understanding sees every day how all growing things on earth open joyfully in spring as the sun draws near, and fall away and wither again in winter as the sun withdraws. What, then, should prevent other similar natural occurrences on earth—namely rain, cold, warmth, fertility, crop failure, peace, and war—from likewise being aroused and brought about through the natural order of the planets created by God? This certainly does no injury to God in his divine power. He nevertheless remains the ruler and protector of those who hope in him alone and place their trust in him. He can still, independently of the course of the heavens, exalt those who humble themselves before him and humble those who exalt themselves against him. Indeed, so far from anything being taken away from God's power as exercised in his ordinary order, the true and genuine art of astrology rather ascribes that power to almighty God. For true, godly astrology is nothing other than a rule and measuring line of God's ordinary working, which almighty God carries out and accomplishes through his own creation, the heavens and the stars. This does not mean that he has confined and sealed himself within that order as a prisoner, but that, according to his customary course and order, he works and acts through the highest things in this world down to the lowest.

Therefore no devout or upright person need fear the stars or their threats, as the prophet Jeremiah also testifies. The stars certainly portend no evil to the devout; they are also those whose duty it is to fear God their Lord alone. The wicked, however, must always be on their guard, whether the stars are favorable or unfavorable. For even if the stars portend great good fortune in this world, what use is that if through their wickedness they turn such good fortune to their own misfortune? Since this does no injury at all to divine power, but rather explains it in its ordered operation, I have accordingly wished, following the teaching and counsel of those experienced in this art, to make known the inclinations and influences of the stars, signs, and planets for the coming year—not as things that must necessarily happen, but as a warning—and have given them for dissemination in print, for the particular pleasure of Your Worships. In this matter and at all times, I wish to commend myself to Your Worships, my gracious lords in authority, subject to you in humble service and obedience. Given on the day of John the Baptist, the twenty-fourth of June, in the year 1528.

Your Worships' obedient appointed physician,
Dr. Antonius Brelochs.

notes.text: E.F.W., a conventional civic honorific, is rendered 'Your Worships'; the letters and forms of address vary in the source. 'Mayors' renders Stetmeyster. Leybartzet is rendered 'physician' in the subscription; the source identifies an appointed personal physician serving the civic authorities, without specifying a modern municipal office structure.

Astronomey is translated 'astrology' where it names the art defended in this preface. The historical term embraces knowledge of celestial motions and their supposed terrestrial influences; the modern separation of astronomy and astrology should not be imposed on Brelochs's vocabulary. Practica is retained as the name of the prognostication genre.
The source's unclear vnndere in A1v, line 29 is provisionally understood as 'other' and rendered '[other?]'. This translation does not constitute a correction of the German working transcription.

Fürsichtigkeit when applied to God is translated 'providence'. Ordentlich in the discussion of divine power and action is rendered with 'ordinary' or 'ordered' language: Brelochs distinguishes God's customary operation through creation from a limitation of his freedom. No claim is made here that the wording is a formal deployment of the scholastic potentia ordinata/absoluta distinction.

The references to Paul's teaching evoke Romans 11:33–36; the statements concerning Christ and knowledge also recall 1 Corinthians 1:30 and Colossians 2:3. The reference to Jeremiah most naturally recalls Jeremiah 10:2. These are editorial identifications of allusions rather than references supplied in the printed text. The translation follows Brelochs's wording rather than substituting a modern Bible version.

Brachmonat is rendered June. The dedication is dated June 24, 1528, although the forecast year is 1529. The entire continuous body paragraph is encoded as one source-aligned segment, with editorial paragraph breaks in English, to avoid assigning translated clauses to inaccurate line boundaries where the printed German runs across them.

segments.text: To the honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the city of Schwäbisch Hall, my gracious and dear lords.

Honorable, prudent, respected, and wise lords: I first offer Your Worships my most willing and diligent service. Gracious and dear lords, I have once again undertaken, according to my limited understanding, to disclose what the influence of the stars and the disposition of the heavens signify and threaten for us in the year 1531. I have also set this down as briefly as possible in a practica, which I present to Your Worships in the customary manner, with the earnest and humble request that you graciously accept it from me and continue to regard me as commended to your care as your humble, obedient, and willing servant. Calculated and written at Schwäbisch Hall on the twelfth day of June, in the year 1530.

Your Worships’ obedient servant,
Dr. Antonius Brelochs.

notes.text: The opening Erern is awkward in the working transcription; the repeated honorific formula is translated conventionally.
Brachmonat is rendered June. The year forecast is 1531; the dedication is dated 1530.
Practica denotes the annual astrological prognostication, not a practical handbook.

segments.text: To the honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the city of Schwäbisch Hall, my gracious and dear lords.

Honorable, prudent, respected, and wise lords: I first offer Your Worships my most willing and diligent service. Gracious and dear lords, I have once again undertaken, so far as my limited understanding permits, to disclose what the course of the heavens signifies for us in the year 1532, and have condensed it as briefly as possible into a small prognostication. I know no one to whom I could more fittingly dedicate this judgment than Your Worships. I therefore ask that you graciously accept from me these future events, thus briefly assembled, and interpret them with your customary kindness. May you also continue to regard me as commended to your care as your humble and willing servant. Dated on the Sunday after St. Bartholomew’s Day, the twenty-seventh of August, in the year 1531.

Your Worships’ obedient servant,
Dr. Antonius Brelochs.

notes.text: Judicium means an astrological judgment or forecast here.
The weekday, feast reference, and date are retained as printed; no calendar conversion is imposed.

segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the city of Schwäbisch Hall, my gracious and dear lords in authority.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent, and wise lords: I first offer Your Worships my most willing and diligent service. Gracious and dear lords in authority, in order to maintain my longstanding custom, I have again undertaken to describe the future events of this present year, fifteen hundred and thirty-five. Accordingly, I have drawn them from the teaching of those learned in the stars and have once again set them down in a practica, which I present to Your Worships in the customary manner. I humbly ask that you graciously accept it from me, interpret it in the most favorable light, and continue to regard me as commended to your care as your humble and willing servant. Dated on the Sunday after St. Pantaleon’s Day, the second of August, in the year 1535 [as printed].

Your Worships’ obedient servant,
Dr. Antonius Brelochs.

notes.text: The dedication prints M. D: XXXV. (1535), as does the alternate Augsburg witness. This potentially problematic date is retained; no correction to 1534 is imposed.
Gebietenden identifies the civic authorities as those who govern or command; it is rendered with “lords in authority.”
The feast reference and numbered day are retained without attempting to reconcile them.

segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the city of Schwäbisch Hall, my gracious and dear lords in authority.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent, and wise lords: I first offer Your Worships my most willing and diligent service. Gracious and dear lords in authority, I have once again undertaken, according to my limited understanding, to disclose what the influences of the stars and the disposition of the heavens signify and threaten for us in the year 1538. I have thus set this down and assembled it as briefly as possible in a prognostication, which I dedicate and present to Your Worships in the customary manner, with the earnest and humble request that you graciously accept it from me and, with your customary kindness, interpret it in the most favorable light. May you also continue to regard me as commended to your care as your humble and willing servant. Given on St. Margaret’s Day, the thirteenth day of July, in the year 1537.

Your Worships’ obedient servant,
Dr. Antonius Brelochs.

notes.text: Hewmonat is rendered July. Both the feast reference and its printed numbered date are retained.
The contracted signature Anthonꝰ is represented by the conventional Latin form Antonius; this is a translation convention, not a change to the German witness.

segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the city of Schwäbisch Hall, my gracious and beloved lords in authority.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent, and wise lords: I first offer Your Worships my entirely willing and diligent service. Gracious and beloved lords in authority: Since through daily experience we learn and see that this lower world, including human beings, irrational animals, stones, plants, and the like, is governed by the stars and the course of the heavens, it is surely fitting that this noble art of astrology should be accepted among the other arts and in no way held in contempt—as so often happens at the hands of certain envious, garrulous people.

That we human beings are governed by the stars needs little or no proof when we carefully observe and consider the nature and character of one person and then another whose time of birth is known, finding them inclined according to the nature and tendency of this or that planet. I speak here only of the tendency and influence of the stars, and not of their coercion or compulsion, since we well know that the stars only incline and do not compel. We may also observe moonstruck, mentally deranged people, who rage more at one time than at another according to the movements of the moon and the other stars. Likewise, people's illnesses and ailments increase or diminish according to the tendency and influence of the stars. Teachers of medicine discover this daily, provided that they have experience of this art of the stars, as Hippocrates and Galen teach and require. The flowers of chicory, too, habitually and for the most part turn toward the sun.

If one also asks all physicians and masters of natural philosophy [what] the reason is that a magnet attracts iron, or that an emerald breaks in the presence of unchastity because it cannot endure it, or again what makes turpeth, rhubarb, and many other plants, roots, seeds, and the like purge and expel, and so forth, they do not say that this happens because these things are cold, hot, moist, or dry. Rather, they say that its cause lies in the celestial powers, which have infused into them a secret nature, hidden from us, through which they possess a particular efficacy—as Mesue testifies in the book on the Consolation of Medicine.

Since, then, all this makes it sufficiently clear that every physician ought to have experience and knowledge of the art of the stars, as Hippocrates, Galen, Rhazes, and Guarinus teach and require, I, although the least among them, have once again, following the old custom and in humble service to Your Worships, compiled as briefly as possible a prognostication from the aforesaid art. In it I indicate what good and evil the stars portend for us in the coming year 1542. I ask Your Worships to receive it and interpret it in the best light, and to keep me, your poor and humble servant, in your care. Given at Schwäbisch Hall on St. Ulrich's Day, in the year 1541.
Your Worships' obedient servant, Antonius Brelochs, Doctor of Medicine.

notes.text: The honorific E.F.W. is rendered 'Your Worships'; the expanded opening addresses the recipients' prudent wisdom (ewer fürsichtig(en) weyßheyt). Stettmayster is rendered 'mayors'; the precise distribution of civic offices is not established by this translation.

Astronomia is translated 'astrology' where it denotes the knowledge of stellar influences and prognostication defended in this passage. Brelochs's historical terminology overlaps the fields now distinguished as astronomy and astrology. The 'wandering star' in line 17 is rendered 'planet.'

The German syntax of lines 11–17 inserts the noncompulsion qualification inside the claim needing little or no proof. The English moves that qualification into a following sentence, preserving its scope while making the passage readable.

At line 25 the working transcription marks vrs as unclear. The scan appears to show an abbreviated form resembling wz, plausibly was ('what'). The translation therefore supplies '[what]' explicitly as a tentative reading; the German TEI has not been altered.

The medical, botanical, and mineral examples are translated as the author's historical assertions. 'Moonstruck' renders Monsüchten, retaining its asserted lunar connection. Turbit is rendered 'turpeth,' the purgative drug, and Reubarbarum as 'rhubarb.'

'Consolation of Medicine' is a literal working rendering of the title or description attributed to Mesue (lines 32–33), not a verified identification of an edition or treatise. The abbreviated d̃ is understood as the article belonging to von der tröstung. Guarinus is retained without an unverified identification.
St. Ulrich's Day conventionally falls on July 4. The translation retains the printed feast-day dating rather than inserting an independently verified publication date.

segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the city of Schwäbisch Hall, my gracious and beloved lords in authority.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent, and wise lords: first I offer Your Worships my entirely willing and diligent service. Gracious and beloved lords in authority,

Claudius Ptolemy of Pelusium, a highly renowned teacher in the art of the stars, writes and explains in his little book of a hundred sayings that the changes of the bodies of this lower world, now into one state and then into another, take place through the revolutions and changes of the heavenly bodies and through their influence. We see this daily and have now experienced it for many years: the movement and courses of the seven planets and other heavenly stars have caused many great uprisings, wars, severe and deadly epidemics, as well as terrible and prolonged dearth, fire, envy, hatred, and other such evils.

Many people have sufficiently reported and indicated these things as warnings in past years. Yet no one has taken all this to heart up to now, nor does anyone do so even now. Rather, the more we are warned—and especially the more earnestly we are exhorted and rebuked in church because of our wicked, grievous, and sinful lives—the more slowly and less readily we set about amending our lives; instead, we are continually found to be more obstinate. Similar things happened frequently in the times of the prophets, and greater and more notable calamity and harm generally followed, as Holy Scripture sufficiently shows and gives us to understand in many places.

Accordingly, once again, to please Your Worships humbly, for your benefit and for everyone's welfare, I have described in this prognostication of mine what future good or evil the stars threaten and indicate for us in this year 1547.

I ask Your Worships to receive and interpret as favorably as possible this prognostication, thus composed as briefly as possible, and to keep me, your poor and humble servant, in your gracious care. To make it clearer and easier to understand, I have divided it, as briefly as possible, into eight chapters. Given at Schwäbisch Hall on St. Sophia's Day, the fifteenth of May, in the year 1546.
Your Worships' obedient servant, Antonius Brelochs, Doctor of Medicine.

notes.text: The civic honorific E.F.W. is rendered 'Your Worships'; it functions as a collective form of address to the magistrates, rather than a claim about their individual wisdom. Stetmeyster is rendered 'mayors'.
The 'little book of a hundred sayings' is the work Brelochs attributes to Ptolemy. The translation preserves that attribution without independently establishing its authorship.
Theurung denotes dearth or scarcity expressed in high prices. 'Dearth' preserves the economic sense without restricting the term to complete famine.

The source's final relative clause about the eight chapters is loosely attached after the request for protection. The translation makes the intended reference to the prognostication explicit by starting a new sentence.

segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the praiseworthy city of Schwäbisch Hall in the Holy Roman Empire, my gracious and beloved lords in authority.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent, and wise lords: first I offer Your Worships my entirely willing and diligent service. Gracious and beloved lords in authority,

Ptolemy, a highly renowned teacher in the art of the stars, explains and describes in his little book of a hundred sayings how the changes of the bodies of this lower world, now into one state and then into another, take place through the revolutions and changes of the heavenly bodies. We see this daily and have now experienced it for many years: the courses of the seven wandering stars and of other stars have caused many great uprisings, violent wars, severe and deadly epidemics, and terrible and prolonged dearth. Although many people sufficiently indicated and reported these things as warnings some years ago, no one has taken them to heart up to now; instead, people have continually become more obstinate, just as similar things happened frequently in the times of the prophets, etc.

Accordingly, once again, to please Your Worships humbly, for everyone's benefit and for the welfare of the German nation as a whole, I have undertaken to describe as briefly as possible in this prognostication of mine what good or evil the stars indicate and threaten for us in this year 1557. I ask Your Worships to receive this from me and interpret it as favorably as possible, and to keep me, your humble servant, in your gracious care.
Given at Schwäbisch Hall on St. Medard's Day, the eighth of June, in the year [15]56, expressed in abbreviated form.
Your Worships' obedient servant, Antonius Brelochs, Doctor of Medicine.

notes.text: The civic honorific E.F.W. is rendered 'Your Worships', a collective form of address to the magistrates; Stetmaystern is rendered 'mayors'.

The seven 'wandering stars' are the seven planets of the historical cosmological scheme, including the sun and moon. This vocabulary is retained rather than converted into the modern astronomical classification.
The phrase '56.der mindern zale' gives a shortened year. The supplied century in '[15]56' makes the date readable while marking what is not printed in full.

The little book of a hundred sayings is attributed to Ptolemy by Brelochs; the attribution is translated without independent authentication. Thewrung is rendered 'dearth', retaining the sense of scarcity and high prices.

segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise mayors and council of the praiseworthy city of Schwäbisch Hall in the Holy Roman Empire, my gracious and beloved lords in authority.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent, and wise lords: first I offer Your Worships my entirely willing and diligent service. Gracious and beloved lords,

The heavenly powers have been created by divine ordinance, and they cannot be prevented from truly coming to pass and appearing. That this is so may be recognized by careful attention. Who among earthly beings can prevent the daily movements and revolutions of the heavens? What earthly person has such great power that he could reverse the course of the sun, which proceeds against the primary movement of the heavens, and turn it backward? Who could change the courses of the other planets—which at one time move forward and at another backward—into different movements? Who could have such authority that, when the sun and moon come together at the Dragon's Head or Tail, he could forbid and prevent the sun from hiding its light and radiance from us? What person has such great power that he could prevent the shadowing of the moon when it is full near the Dragon's Head or Tail? Truly, no one except almighty God, our Creator, alone.

These things are the footprints of our Redeemer, according to the testimony of the holy teacher Gregory. When we see them, we marvel not only at his strength and power, but still more at his wonderful works, wisdom, and inexpressible goodness and generosity.

Truly, they are wonderful works: through divine creation the noble lights, sun and moon, together with the other stars, have by no means been placed in the heavens in vain. These lower things are moved through the indications of the higher stars, at one time by mortality, at another by dearth, and at another by wars, etc. Such things might also appear in great number and often, if a counteracting cause of the higher bodies did not at times resist and overcome such indications.

In the same way, a magnet always draws iron to itself; but if it is smeared with garlic juice, its power is taken away. An animal's wound would also fester if it were not helped with salves and medicines. So too the stars would sometimes bring about terrible occurrences if a stronger and more powerful cause did not encounter and oppose them.

For this reason, sailors at sea always steer by the stars. Farmers and shepherds likewise observe the configuration of the moon and heavens in the conception of livestock and in the sowing and planting of crops, to avoid suffering harm from unfortunate and evil occurrences. For, as Ptolemy explains, a wise man can prevent much evil that would otherwise come through the stars if he investigates the nature and properties of the stars.

On this basis I have once again undertaken to arrange a prognostication for the coming year, as briefly as possible, indicating what good or evil the stars signify for us in that year according to the course of nature.
Given at Schwäbisch Hall on the feast of John the Baptist, in the year 1557.

Your Worships’ obedient servant,
Dr. Antonius Brelochs.

notes.text: The source marks only the final n of lieben in the salutation as unclear. This grammatical uncertainty does not affect the English 'beloved'. E.F.W. is rendered 'Your Worships', a collective civic honorific; Stätmeystern is rendered 'mayors'.

The Dragon's Head and Tail are the ascending and descending lunar nodes. The translation preserves the historical names. The 'primary movement' refers to the overarching daily motion of the heavens within the cosmology assumed by the author.

At A2v, lines 12–14, 'ein widerwertige vrsach der öbersten Cörper' is syntactically difficult. 'A counteracting cause of the higher bodies' closely preserves the transmitted construction. It may describe a countervailing celestial cause or a cause acting against the higher bodies' indications; the translation does not decide its exact physical location. The subsequent sentence explicitly says that a stronger cause may oppose the stars' effects.

The claims about garlic inhibiting magnetism and about celestial influences are translated as historical assertions. The translation does not substitute modern explanations. Sterben in the catalogue of calamities is rendered 'mortality'; the context may particularly evoke widespread deaths or epidemic mortality.

The translation retains the attribution to the holy teacher Gregory without supplying an unverified work or passage. The initial inability to prevent heavenly movements is distinguished in the source itself from the later possibility of counteracting their indicated earthly effects.

segments.text: To the steadfast, honorable, prudent, respected, and wise lords, the mayors and council of the praiseworthy city of Schwäbisch Hall in the Holy Roman Empire, my gracious lords in authority.

Steadfast, honorable, prudent, and wise lords: I first offer Your Worships my most willing and diligent service. Gracious and dear lords, so as not to depart from my longstanding practice and custom, I have once again undertaken, according to my limited understanding, to set down and write something concerning the courses, revolutions, influences, and positions of the planets, together with their natural inclinations, for the coming year 1559. I have thus composed, assembled, condensed, and arranged this as briefly as possible in a prognostication, which I deliver and submit to Your Worships in the customary manner. I humbly ask that Your Worships graciously accept it from me, interpret it in the most favorable light, and graciously continue to regard me as commended to your care as your humble and willing servant.

Given at Schwäbisch Hall on St. George’s Day, the twenty-third day of April, in the year 1558.

So that this practica of mine may be understood more clearly, I have divided it into eight chapters.

Your Worships’ obedient servant,
Dr. Antonius Brelochs.

notes.text: The forecast year is 1559; the dedication is dated April 23, 1558.
The eight-chapter statement is included because the transcription includes it before the signature.
The signature’s spelling Brellochs is normalized to Brelochs in English; the source spelling is retained in the German TEI.
